help.intro: weil (because) opens a subordinate clause, and a subordinate clause in German sends its conjugated verb to the very end: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin — not 'weil ich bin krank'. This is the single biggest word-order rule after verb-second, and it will run through every level from here: dass, wenn, ob, obwohl, als and every relative clause do the same. A comma always separates the two clauses. In the Perfekt the helper goes last, after the participle: …, weil ich gestern lange gearbeitet habe. With a modal, the modal goes last: …, weil ich arbeiten muss. Learn it physically — 'the conjunction kicks the verb to the back' — and say a weil-sentence aloud every day until the kick is automatic. Five sentences here have two gaps — the infinitive or participle first, then the modal or helper as the very last word.
help.tips[0].title: weil … verb at the end, comma before
help.tips[0].text: Main clause, comma, weil, subject, everything else, verb. Ich nehme den Bus, weil es regnet. Sie lernt Deutsch, weil sie in Berlin wohnt.
help.tips[0].examples[0].en: I'm staying at home because I'm ill.
help.tips[0].examples[1].en: We're not buying a car because we have no money.
help.tips[0].trap: English keeps 'because I am ill'. German: 'weil ich krank bin'. The verb is the last word, every time.
help.tips[0].check.q: Ich trage heute eine Jacke, weil ____. (standard written German)
help.tips[0].check.why: weil starts a subordinate clause, so the conjugated verb ist goes to the very end: weil es kalt ist.
help.tips[0].visual.caption: weil sends the verb to the very end of its clause.
help.tips[1].title: Two verbs? Both at the end, helper last
help.tips[1].text: Perfekt: …, weil ich gestern lange gearbeitet habe. Modal: …, weil ich morgen früh aufstehen muss. Separable verbs rejoin: …, weil der Zug um neun abfährt.
help.tips[1].examples[0].en: I'm tired because I slept badly.
help.tips[1].examples[1].en: He's not coming because he has to work.
help.tips[1].check.q: Sie ist nicht im Büro, weil sie zum Arzt ____.
help.tips[1].check.why: Both verbs go to the end, and the conjugated modal comes last: gehen muss.
help.tips[2].text: denn also means because but is a plain connector: verb stays second (…, denn ich bin krank). weil is a subordinator: verb last. Both are correct; weil is far more common in speech.
help.tips[2].examples[1].en: I'm not coming, because I have no time.
help.tips[2].check.why: denn is a plain connector: subject, then the verb in second place, just like a main clause. Only weil sends the verb to the end.
help.tips[3].title: The conjunction kicks the verb to the back
help.tips[3].text: Say weil and kick with your foot. The verb flies to the end. Pair the gesture with the word for a week and the order will feel wrong the other way.
help.tips[3].examples[0].en: I'm staying at home because I'm ill.
help.tips[3].examples[1].en: He is tired because he slept badly.
help.tips[3].check.q: Ich beeile mich, weil der Zug gleich ____.
help.tips[3].check.why: weil kicks the whole verb to the end, and a separable verb joins up again there: abfährt.
help.remember[0]: weil = verb last. No exceptions, no matter how long the clause.
help.remember[1]: Helper or modal? It goes even later: gearbeitet habe, aufstehen muss.
help.context.en: Why aren't you coming to the party? – I'm not coming because I have to get up early tomorrow. And my brother isn't coming because he's ill. – A pity! Lisa isn't coming either, because she doesn't feel like it. – Then the three of us will celebrate, because we have time!
help.mistakes[0].why: The subordinate verb goes to the end.
help.mistakes[1].why: The helper is the very last word.
help.hook: Give your reasons in German: after weil the verb flies to the very end — weil ich krank bin, never weil ich bin krank.
categories[0].label: weil + Verb am Ende
sentences[0].english: I'm staying home because I'm ill.
sentences[0].why: weil kicks the verb to the clause's end: ich krank BIN.
sentences[1].english: She learns German because she lives in Berlin.
sentences[1].why: In the weil-clause the verb goes last: sie in Berlin WOHNT.
sentences[2].english: We take the bus because it's raining today.
sentences[2].why: weil + subject + rest + verb last: es heute REGNET.
sentences[3].english: He is tired because he slept badly.
sentences[3].why: With Perfekt, the helper goes very last: geschlafen HAT — participle before it.
sentences[4].english: I buy the book because it is interesting.
sentences[4].why: Verb to the end: es interessant IST.
sentences[5].english: He goes to the doctor because he has a fever.
sentences[5].why: weil sends hat to the end: er Fieber HAT.
sentences[6].english: I study a lot because I want to pass the exam.
sentences[6].why: With a modal, the modal goes last: bestehen WILL — infinitive before it.
sentences[7].english: We stay inside because it is cold.
sentences[8].english: Because I'm on holiday, I'm happy.
sentences[8].why: A fronted weil-clause fills position 1, so the main clause starts with its verb: bin ich glücklich.
sentences[9].english: I eat an apple because I am hungry.
sentences[10].english: He is late because the bus didn't come.
sentences[10].why: Perfekt in the weil-clause: participle, then the helper last — gekommen IST.
sentences[11].english: She is staying at home today because she has to work.
sentences[11].why: The modal takes the last seat: arbeiten MUSS.
sentences[12].english: Because I have a question, I'm calling you.
sentences[12].why: The weil-clause comes first with its verb at ITS end; the main clause then starts verb-first: Weil ich eine Frage habe, rufe ich …
sentences[13].english: She wears a jacket because it is windy.
sentences[14].english: He saves money because he wants to buy a car.
sentences[15].english: I don't drink coffee in the evening because otherwise I can't sleep.
sentences[15].why: The modal closes the clause: schlafen KANN — sonst 'otherwise' stays inside.
sentences[16].english: She is so happy because she's passed the exam.
sentences[16].why: Perfekt: participle then helper at the very end — bestanden HAT.
sentences[17].english: Because the train is delayed, we are taking a taxi.
sentences[17].why: After a fronted weil-clause the main clause inverts: nehmen wir ein Taxi.
sentences[18].english: Lisa isn't here any more because she has gone home.
sentences[18].why: Perfekt with sein: gegangen IST — the helper takes the last position.
